section_summary: This section traces Japanese regulation of opium and other narcotics in the Kwantung Leased Territory from the 1922 opium-corruption judgments through the 1924 Opium Law, its enforcement rules, the 1927 narcotics-control regulation, and the 1928 government monopoly. Consular reports describe licensing of Chinese addicts and retailers, official revenue from opium, weaknesses in enforcement, and allegations that Dairen served as a major narcotics-smuggling entrepôt. The final documents investigate large imports of morphine-containing “benzoline” and begin a September 1930 report on the resulting criminal case.

subfiles.title: File jacket: Traffic in Narcotics in Kwantung
subfiles.about: The jacket identifies the case as concerning traffic in narcotics in Kwantung.
subfiles.summary: File jacket "Traffic in Narcotics in Kwantung," opened August 11, 1922, with filing and handling instructions.

subfiles.title: Dairen Despatch No. 25: Judgments in Opium Scandal
subfiles.about: The consul forwards a newspaper clipping reporting the judgments in the Kwantung opium scandal.
subfiles.summary: Dairen Despatch 25 lists prison sentences for Koga, Nakano, Obata and Kajii in the opium scandal and 841,026.78 yen recovered civilly; the consul finds the sentences surprisingly lenient.

subfiles.title: Judgments Rendered in Opium Case
subfiles.about: The clipping reports the criminal sentences and civil findings arising from fraudulent administration of the Kwantung opium trade.
subfiles.summary: Ryojun District Court sentenced Koga, Nakano, Obata and Kajii, acquitted six others and ordered large repayments; officials manipulated opium prices through nominal purchasers so associates profited at the government's expense, Koga demanded Dairen exchange shares, and the monopoly's legal basis is questionable.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 379-E: Proposed Kwantung Opium Regulations
subfiles.from: Cyrus E. Woods, American Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The ambassador reports cabinet approval of regulations intended to control opium production, sale, and use in Kwantung.
subfiles.summary: Proposed system would register confirmed addicts to buy limited quantities from licensed dealers, with the register eventually closed; Woods ties it to outrage over the 1921 opium scandal profiting officials and a nominal charity, and will forward the regulations once published.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 399-E: Transmission of Imperial Ordinance No. 53
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, for the American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy transmits a translation of the newly promulgated Kwantung Province Opium Regulations.
subfiles.summary: Caffery encloses Imperial Ordinance 53, promulgated March 26, 1924, noting its effective date is left to the Governor-General of Kwantung.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 53: Kwantung Province Opium Regulations
subfiles.about: The ordinance prohibits unauthorized opium use and commerce and establishes penalties and regulatory exceptions.
subfiles.summary: Ordinance 53 defines opium, bars smoking or eating it except by authorized addicts, bans opium halls and poppy cultivation and restricts manufacture, trade and possession, with limited exceptions for physicians and dealers, penalties up to seven years' penal servitude, and the Governor-General setting the effective date.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Sturgeon’s Reporting
subfiles.about: The memorandum defends Vice Consul Sturgeon against Consul General Stewart’s criticism of his account of Japanese legislative procedure.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Sturgeon reasonably began translating the opium measure after it appeared in the press and correctly saw Privy Council approval as practically decisive; Stewart's constitutional objection is overly formal, and Sturgeon better understood Japanese procedure.

subfiles.title: Dairen Despatch No. 90: Kwantung Leased Territory Opium Act
subfiles.from: American Vice Consul in Charge at Dairen
subfiles.about: The vice consul forwards the text of the new opium act and discusses its anticipated implementation.
subfiles.summary: Dairen Despatch 90: the Privy Council approved the measure March 15, the Governor hasn't fixed its effective date, and his press statement promised treaty compatibility, strict prevention of new addiction and closely limited supplies for existing addicts; enforcement will need preparation.

subfiles.title: New Opium Act: Its Chief Features
subfiles.about: The clipping summarizes the principal prohibitions, exceptions, and penalties in the proposed Kwantung opium act.
subfiles.summary: Article "New Opium Act": defines covered opium types, limits smoking to permitted confirmed addicts, regulates opium, medicinal preparations and paraphernalia, bans opium houses and poppy cultivation, authorizes inspections and reporting, lists penalties, and leaves the start date to the Governor.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Department on Japanese Legislative Procedure
subfiles.from: Nathaniel B. Stewart, American Consul General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Stewart criticizes Sturgeon’s statement that the Privy Council had “passed” the Kwantung Opium Act.
subfiles.summary: Stewart says the Privy Council merely approved the bill, the Throne wasn't constitutionally required to refer it there, and promulgation under the Imperial Sign Manual on March 26 was the essential act.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Kwantung Drug-Control Despatches to the Treasury
subfiles.about: The State Department sends the Treasury copies of the Tokyo and Dairen reports on Kwantung drug-control regulations.
subfiles.summary: Letter sends the Treasury Tokyo Despatch 399-E (April 2) and Dairen Despatch 90 (March 31) with enclosures, for Colonel L. G. Nutt.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Kwantung Drug-Control Despatches to Commerce
subfiles.about: The State Department sends the Commerce Department copies of the Tokyo and Dairen reports on Kwantung drug regulation.
subfiles.summary: Letter sends Commerce the embassy's April 2 and Dairen consulate's March 31 despatches with enclosures on habit-forming-drug controls.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 613-E: Effective Date of the New Opium Act
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, American Embassy at Karuizawa
subfiles.about: Caffery reports that the Kwantung opium act will take effect on September 1, 1924.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo Despatch 613-E supplements 399-E: Japanese authorities announced September 1 as the new opium act's effective date in the leased territory.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 613-E to Commerce
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards the embassy report announcing implementation of the Kwantung opium regulations.
subfiles.summary: Note sends Commerce Despatch 613-E of August 19, 1924 from Tokyo on implementation of the opium act.

subfiles.title: Dairen Despatch No. 104: Regulations for Enforcement of the Opium Act
subfiles.from: American Vice Consul in Charge at Dairen
subfiles.about: The vice consul forwards the official regulations implementing the Kwantung Opium Act from September 1, 1924.
subfiles.summary: The report identifies the rules as Kwantung Government Ordinance No. 50 and notes that little information was yet available about practical enforcement. It predicts difficulty because restrictions would affect many Chinese addicts and people who profited from the trade. The Chinese population principally affected is estimated at 89,882.

subfiles.title: Regulations for Enforcement of the Kwantung Leased Territory Opium Act
subfiles.about: The regulations establish the permit, supply, accounting, inspection, and penalty system governing addicts and the opium trade.
subfiles.summary: Chinese addicts must apply for smoking permits, undergo medical examination, and observe ten-day purchase and possession limits. Dealers, retailers, pharmacists, and medical practitioners are regulated through licenses, designated supply channels, import restrictions through Dairen, account books, and monthly reports. The rules prescribe penalties, representative liability, license suspension, and simultaneous commencement with the Opium Law.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 104 to Commerce
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards Dairen Despatch No. 104 and its enforcement-regulation enclosure to Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Note sends Commerce the September 5 consular report, Despatch 104, on enforcing the Kwantung Leased Territory Opium Act.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 104 to the Treasury
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards Dairen Despatch No. 104 and its enclosure to the Treasury.
subfiles.summary: Letter sends the Treasury Despatch 104 on regulations enforcing the Kwantung Opium Act, for Colonel L. G. Nutt.

subfiles.title: Federal Narcotics Control Board Acknowledgment
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary, Federal Narcotics Control Board
subfiles.about: The Board acknowledges receipt of the State Department’s transmittal concerning Kwantung opium regulations.
subfiles.summary: The Federal Narcotics Control Board acknowledges the October communication and Dairen Despatch 104, delayed because Treasury misrouted the material.

subfiles.title: Dairen Despatch No. 256: Kwantung Regulation No. 54
subfiles.from: D. Sturgeon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Sturgeon transmits the new Kwantung regulation governing narcotics other than opium.
subfiles.summary: Regulation No. 54 replaces Regulation No. 5 of 1918 and is described as substantially more comprehensive and centralized. It places import and export licensing directly under the Governor and requires detailed applications. The measure took effect October 1, 1927, and the consulate planned a later report on its effects.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Government Regulation No. 54: Control of Narcotics
subfiles.about: The regulation controls the manufacture, import, export, sale, delivery, and possession of morphine, cocaine, and similar drugs.
subfiles.summary: Regulation 54: manufacture and international movement of narcotics need the Governor's permission, with applications giving drug, quantity, route, date, purpose and parties; dealers keep records three years for inspection; transshipment counts as import or export; penalties and employer liability set; 1918 rules canceled, with transitional protection for prior contracts.

subfiles.title: Supplemental Dairen Report on the Effect of Regulation No. 54
subfiles.about: The consul evaluates the anticipated effectiveness of the new Kwantung narcotics regulation.
subfiles.summary: Dairen report: old rules covered only morphine and cocaine, letting heroin, peronin and benzoline in without permits and embarrassing authorities when British firms were investigated; officials expect the broader rule to control the trade, critics find penalties too light, and reputational damage may deter respectable firms.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 632: Alleged Japanese Drug Factory at Port Arthur
subfiles.from: William R. Castle, Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department requests investigation of a report that a Japanese factory at Port Arthur produced drugs far beyond China’s legitimate needs.
subfiles.summary: Instruction 632: a National Anti-Opium Association of China claim, in an August 29, 1929 Japan Weekly Chronicle report, of a Japanese drug factory at Port Arthur; State asks whether it's true and what drugs and quantities are made.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 1373: Inquiry into the Alleged Port Arthur Factory
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville reports the results of an inquiry into the alleged narcotics factory at Port Arthur.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 1373: the Kwantung Opium Monopoly Bureau told Consul Langdon its Dairen laboratory, preparing crude opium for licensed addicts, is the territory's only licensed narcotics maker, so Neville thinks the allegation misidentified it; Langdon's December 9 report and enclosures are cited.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 2: Request for Copies of Langdon’s December 9 Despatch
subfiles.about: The Department requests five copies of the missing Dairen despatch and its enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Instruction 2: State apparently never received Langdon's report on narcotics control in the Kwantung Leased Territory and directs the ambassador to send five copies with enclosures promptly.

subfiles.title: Dairen Letter: Narcotic Traffic Notes
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Langdon reports on a major smuggling investigation, the official opium business, and destruction of seized opium at Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Langdon says Dairen’s free-port procedures, large unexamined cargo volume, and easy passenger departures made it an attractive narcotics entrepôt serving Shanghai, Tientsin, and northern markets. He notes European and Japanese involvement, substantial Persian-opium imports, and profitable Opium Monopoly Bureau operations. A final item reports the public burning at Mukden of opium seized while being mailed from Hamburg to Changchun.

subfiles.title: Most Extensive Smuggling Plots
subfiles.about: The clipping reports a police investigation into large-scale narcotics smuggling involving prominent Japanese suspects.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary article on smuggling plots evading Kwantung's narcotics transitional clause: large benzoline deliveries by post since 1928, groups including former Diet member T. Shirakawa and K. Matsuushi, and the respectable standing of several implicated firms or individuals.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Langdon for Complete Smuggling Enclosure and Clarification of “Benzoin”
subfiles.from: William R. Castle, Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: William R. Langdon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: The Department requests the missing pages of the smuggling clipping and clarification of the substance called “benzoin.”
subfiles.summary: State got only one page of the June 4 newspaper enclosure and asks Langdon for the full item; since benzoin isn't ordinarily a narcotic, it asks whether the term concealed another drug and what shipments contained, and encourages sharing information with East Asian posts.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 199: Langdon Letter on Dairen as a Drug-Distribution Center
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville forwards Langdon’s letter on the alleged use of Dairen as a distribution center for illicit opium and other drugs.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo Despatch 199 transmits the Dairen consul Langdon's June 23 letter on Dairen as a distribution center for illicit narcotics.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Despatch No. 199 and Transmission of the July 31 Instruction
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Neville’s despatch and supplies a copy of its instruction to Langdon.
subfiles.summary: State acknowledges Despatch 199 with Langdon's June 23 report and forwards its July 31 instruction seeking more details and a complete enclosure.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 94: Renewed Request for the December 9, 1929 Despatch
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department repeats its request for copies of Langdon’s December 9, 1929 report and enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Instruction 94 renews the request for the December 9, 1929 despatch, encloses the earlier February 3 request, and asks the embassy to report who sent copies, or prepare and send them.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 249: Transmission of Five Copies of Langdon’s Report
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville transmits five copies of Langdon’s December 9, 1929 despatch and its enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Neville explains that the embassy had not previously forwarded copies because Langdon’s original stated that one had gone directly to the Department. In compliance with Instruction No. 94, the embassy now sends five copies with enclosures.

subfiles.title: Final-Page Fragment of a Langdon Report on the Opium Monopoly
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: The fragment discusses possible changes to the Kwantung monopoly and the disposition of confiscated morphine.
subfiles.summary: Final-page fragment of a Langdon report: whether morphine seized in Kwantung should be sold for the territorial budget rather than supplied to the monopoly stock in Chosen; placing morphine under monopoly needs further study.

subfiles.title: Incomplete Copy of Langdon’s Despatch on Regulation of Opium Traffic
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: The surviving pages review the history, legal structure, revenue, and consumption of the Kwantung opium system.
subfiles.summary: Langdon traces policy from the 1909 international conference through the Chinese Charity Institute system, the 1924 law, and creation of the Opium Monopoly Bureau in 1928. He reproduces portions of the 1922 corruption judgment and gives tables of fraudulent transactions, monopoly revenue, imports, population, and estimated Chinese per-capita consumption. The report says the government earned a net ¥1,088,115 from opium in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1929, while imports and estimated consumption had risen substantially.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1: Kwantung Leased Territory Opium Law
subfiles.about: The enclosure gives the 1924 Opium Law as amended by Imperial Ordinance No. 167 of 1928.
subfiles.summary: Enclosure 1: the amended law centralizes opium importation, sale, transfer, storage and manufacture under the Governor, with regulated exceptions for retailers, addicts and medical professionals; it bans opium houses, poppy cultivation and unauthorized smoking, with detailed penalties.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: Organization of the Kwantung Government Monopoly Bureau
subfiles.about: Imperial Ordinance No. 179 establishes the Kwantung Government Monopoly Bureau and defines its staff and duties.
subfiles.summary: Enclosure 2: the Kwantung Government Monopoly Bureau, at Dairen under the Governor, controls crude and medicinal opium transactions and custody, staffed by a chief, directors, technical experts and an interpreter.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 3: Revised Regulations for Enforcement of the Kwantung Opium Law
subfiles.about: The enclosure gives the 1924 enforcement regulations as revised for the 1928 monopoly system.
subfiles.summary: Enclosure 3: revised enforcement rules keep permits, medical examinations, purchase limits and licensed retail sales for Chinese addicts, make the Monopoly Bureau the source of crude and medicinal opium, regulate supply, export, records and reporting, set penalties and vicarious liability, and recognize existing druggists.

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Illicit Narcotics Traffic at Dairen
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references an instruction concerning Dairen narcotics traffic and its connections with Hamburg and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to file 893.114 Narcotics/153: Neville on illicit narcotics traffic at Dairen linked to Hamburg and Japan.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Dairen Opium and Smuggling Reports to the Treasury
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Treasury the December 1929 opium report and the June 1930 narcotics-smuggling report.
subfiles.summary: Letter sends the Treasury Tokyo Despatch 249 with Langdon's December 9 report on the Kwantung opium traffic and his June 23 report on Dairen smuggling, noting Dairen's shipping links to American ports and that "benzoin" was probably benzoylmorphine.

subfiles.title: Dairen Despatch No. 184: Narcotic Trafficking at Dairen
subfiles.about: The consul supplies the complete smuggling clipping and explains that its “benzoin” was benzoline containing morphine.
subfiles.summary: Dairen Despatch 184: benzoline, reportedly 80 percent morphine, counts as a narcotic under Regulation 54; defendants kept importing other narcotics via false pre-October 1927 contract claims, about 6,165 kilograms passed the Dairen Post Office through April 1929, the loophole closed January 30, 1930, and defendants were free on bail.
